subtype: Approach: resource and budget planning with fixed-cost-first split [Thinking]
passage: Thomas turned his teacup slowly and said, "Keerthana, when I got my first salary, thirty thousand, I felt rich for about ten minutes. Then I did something a senior taught me. Before spending a rupee, I wrote what I could not avoid: rent, food, bus pass, the phone bill. Then I added them up." He tapped the table. "Seventeen thousand five hundred gone before I even began. What was left was not a fortune. It was the amount I could truly play with." Keerthana raised her eyebrows. "That is exactly what I needed," Thomas went on, "to see the free part small and honest, not big and imaginary. After that I stopped resenting the limit. It was just the truth."

qa.q: How much of the thirty thousand did Thomas find was already gone?
qa.a: Seventeen thousand five hundred was gone before Thomas began spending.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when first receiving the salary?
qa.a: Thomas felt rich for about ten minutes, before adding up the unavoidable costs showed how little was free.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do with her own first salary, and why?
qa.a: Keerthana could list the costs she cannot avoid first and see what remains, because the true free amount is then clear.

qa.q: How might a friend who spent freely in the first month see Thomas's method?
qa.a: That friend might feel it is dull at first but later see that it prevents the shock of an empty account.

grounding: An elder recalls listing unavoidable costs first from a first salary, which showed how little was truly free to spend.

subtype: Approach: pay-yourself-first automation using a standing instruction [Action]
passage: It was salary day and the office celebrated with samosas, but Akash had a different plan for the afternoon. The bank app was slow, the queue of colleagues at the tea counter was loud, and the festival sale ads were already flashing on the phone. First, before the samosas, Akash opened the transfers page and set a standing instruction: twelve percent of the salary into a savings account of its own, on the same day every month, and a small amount into a monthly investment plan. Sumit, at the next desk, asked what the fuss was. "If I decide later, I'll spend it," Akash said. "If it's automatic, the choice is already made." The amount was modest, and the phone stopped nagging.

qa.q: Where does the standing instruction send twelve percent of the salary?
qa.a: It sends twelve percent of the salary into a savings account of its own on the same day every month.

qa.q: Why did Akash set the transfer before spending anything?
qa.a: Akash worried that a later decision would end in spending, and wanted saving to happen by default.

qa.q: What could Akash add if the transfer leaves too little for the month, and why?
qa.a: Akash could lower the fixed amount slightly after checking the month's bills, because a plan that fits is easier to keep. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sumit see Akash's action on salary day?
qa.a: Sumit is curious and may see a habit that removes daily temptation, since the saving has already happened.

grounding: On salary day a graduate sets an automatic transfer to a separate savings account before spending anything, so saving becomes the default.

subtype: Approach: spend freely and see what is left [Pitfall]
passage: In Lagos, Chidi's first pay landed on a Friday, and by Saturday it felt like a fortune. Chidi bought the newest phone on monthly instalments, ate out with colleagues four nights a week, and ordered a new jacket online. Nobody had said no, and no total had ever been set for the month. Sami, sharing the flat, saw the bags arriving and said nothing at first. By the twentieth, the account was empty. Chidi borrowed from Sami for the bus fare and skipped the office lunch. The phone instalment was due in five days. Sitting on the kitchen floor, Chidi wrote the same question three times on a napkin: where did it all go?

qa.q: On which day of the month was the account empty?
qa.a: The account was empty by the twentieth.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling while writing the question on the napkin?
qa.a: Chidi was confused and anxious about where the money had gone, since no total had been set for the month.

qa.q: What could Chidi do at the start of next month, and why?
qa.a: Chidi could set a total for the month and list the bills first, because a limit shows what is safe to spend.

qa.q: How might Sami see lending money for the bus fare?
qa.a: Sami may feel worried and a little uneasy, since Sami saw the bags arrive and now sees the empty account.

grounding: A first-job employee treats the credited amount as plentiful, buys a phone on instalments and eats out often, and runs out before month's end.

subtype: Approach: track spending for a month, then set category limits [Revision]
passage:
Lakshmi: You look stressed. Short again this month?

Jyoti: Third month running. I don't get it. My salary isn't small.

Lakshmi: Do you know where it goes?

Jyoti: Not exactly. So I'm going to write down every payment I make from my phone, for one month. Everything.

(A month later, at the pantry.)

Jyoti: Look at this. Food delivery is the biggest item. More than transport and phone put together.

Lakshmi: Seriously? I would have guessed rent.

Jyoti: Rent is fixed. This is the leak. So now there's a weekly cap on delivery, and cooking twice.

Lakshmi: Easier than a guessed budget.

Jyoti: Yes. Numbers I can see are better than promises I make to myself.

qa.q: Which item was the biggest in Jyoti's month of records?
qa.a: Food delivery was the biggest item, more than transport and phone put together.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when saying that the salary is not small?
qa.a: Jyoti felt puzzled and stressed at being short for the third month in a row.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try if the weekly cap keeps being broken, and why?
qa.a: Jyoti could cook more meals in advance so the cap is easy to keep, since the cap works only when an alternative exists.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see the results compared with the earlier guess about rent?
qa.a: Lakshmi was surprised, because rent had been the guess, which shows how easily a guessed budget can miss the real leak.

grounding: After running short an employee records every payment for a month, finds the biggest leak and sets a weekly cap on it.

subtype: Approach: copying a friend's budget percentages [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Pankaj, and in my first month as an analyst I copied a friend's budget. Vasudha had sent me a video about a fifty-thirty-twenty split: half for needs, thirty for wants, twenty for savings. It looked neat, so I put it in my notes and felt organised. Then the month began. I send a good part of my pay home, and I share a flat with two others, so my rent and bills were far more than half. The wants slice was meaningless. By the tenth I was borrowing from the savings slice to pay for basic things. The rule was fine for someone in a different life. I had never asked whether it fitted mine, and my obligations did not fit inside those three boxes.

qa.q: Which friend sent Pankaj the video about the split?
qa.a: Vasudha sent Pankaj the video about the fifty-thirty-twenty split.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel at the start of the month after copying the rule?
qa.a: Pankaj felt organised and pleased at first, before finding that the split did not fit real life.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do instead of copying a rule, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could begin with the money sent home and the shared rent and see what remains, because the plan then reflects real duties.

qa.q: How might the family at home see the money Pankaj sends?
qa.a: The family probably relies on the money and may worry if it were cut to fit a rule that ignores them.

grounding: An analyst copies a popular percentage split from a video without noticing family remittances and shared housing make it unrealistic.

subtype: Approach: buffer planning with an emergency fund target [Thinking]
passage: In the office pantry in Gurugram, Lalremsiami stared at a chart of the month and asked Swati, who sat two desks away, how she coped when money surprised her. "It doesn't surprise me much now," Swati said. Lalremsiami thought about it that evening. First goal: a month's expenses put away, untouched. Then three months. Only after that would anything go towards investing. The reason was simple. A sudden bill, whether for the doctor, a phone repair or a train home, would then be an annoyance and not a loan. Lalremsiami opened a separate account, named it "cushion", and made the first small deposit. A person at the bank could explain the products, but the order of priorities was already clear.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami name the new account?
qa.a: Lalremsiami named the new account cushion.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami think about the order of goals?
qa.a: Lalremsiami thought a cushion should come before investing, so that a sudden bill would be an annoyance and not a loan.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do to check the plan with expert help, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami could talk to a qualified adviser at the bank about personal choices, because general reasoning still needs checking against real numbers.

qa.q: How might Swati see the question about coping with surprises?
qa.a: Swati may feel glad to share an experience and see it as a sign that Lalremsiami is starting to plan ahead.

grounding: An employee makes a one-month and then three-month emergency cushion the first goal before any investing, so a shock does not become a loan.

subtype: Approach: envelope-style split into separate accounts [Action]
passage: Note from the first-job orientation mentor. Rafiq joined the company in July and I watched how the salary was handled on the first day it arrived. Within two hours Rafiq had moved money into three places: a bills account that pays rent and the phone, a spending wallet for food and outings, and a savings pot. Madhuri, another new joiner, asked what happens when the wallet runs out early. "Then I wait," Rafiq said. "I don't touch the other two." By the last week of the month the wallet was empty and Rafiq walked to the office instead of taking the auto. It was a small inconvenience. I noted that the bills were paid on time and the savings pot had not moved.

qa.q: How many places did Rafiq split the salary into?
qa.a: Rafiq split the salary into three places: a bills account, a spending wallet and a savings pot.

qa.q: What did Rafiq mean by saying I wait when the wallet was empty?
qa.a: Rafiq meant that Rafiq would not dip into the other two pots and would put up with the inconvenience until next month.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do if the spending wallet is always empty early, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could adjust the wallet's share slightly after two months of data, because the split should match real needs.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Rafiq's rule of waiting?
qa.a: Madhuri seems curious, and may find it strict but clear, since the other pots stay safe.

grounding: A new employee divides the salary the same day into a bills account, a spending wallet and a savings pot, and waits when the wallet is empty.

subtype: Approach: values-first planning about family obligations [Thinking]
passage: Sabina, Himani's aunt, put down her knitting and said, "Before your first salary arrives, decide what comes first. When I began work, I sat with a pen and wrote: a fixed amount every month for your grandparents, and your cousin's tuition. Before clothes, before outings. Then I looked at what was left." She smiled. "Naming what mattered most made the rest easier. I stopped feeling guilty about the outings, because I knew the important things were already paid. And when I wanted something expensive, I could say honestly, 'I will wait, that is not a priority right now.'" Himani asked quietly, "Did you ever regret it?" "Never. It was my own decision, not one forced on me."

qa.q: What two things did Sabina put first in her plan?
qa.a: Sabina put a fixed monthly amount for the grandparents and the cousin's tuition first.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel about the outings after naming what mattered most?
qa.a: Sabina stopped feeling guilty about the outings, because the important things were already paid.

qa.q: What could Himani do before her first salary, and why?
qa.a: Himani could write which duties she wants to honour and how much each needs, because deciding first makes later trade-offs calmer.

qa.q: How might the cousin see the tuition money?
qa.a: The cousin probably feels supported and secure about tuition, though may not know how much thought went into it.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding that fixed support for family and a relative's tuition comes before lifestyle spending, which made trade-offs easier.

subtype: Approach: review every quarter and adjust for raises and rent hikes [Revision]
passage: In Cape Town, the appraisal letter came in March, and the landlord's message about a rent rise arrived a week later. Zanele opened the budget file that had not been touched since August. "It was a plan for the old me," Zanele said to Lucia, a colleague at lunch. The raise was modest and the rent rise took most of it. So Zanele added half of the raise to the monthly savings transfer, trimmed two subscriptions that nobody used, and moved a few dates for bills. The whole revision took forty minutes. Lucia asked why bother. "A budget isn't a contract," Zanele replied. "If life changes, the plan should too, and I check every three months."

qa.q: When did the appraisal letter arrive?
qa.a: The appraisal letter came in March.

qa.q: What did Zanele think about the old budget file?
qa.a: Zanele felt it was a plan for the old self, and saw that it needed an update after the raise and the rent rise.

qa.q: What could Zanele do if the next rent rise is larger, and why?
qa.a: Zanele could review what can be trimmed first and then ask whether a shared flat is possible, because the plan needs to fit new costs.

qa.q: How might Lucia see the quarterly check?
qa.a: Lucia may find it careful and a bit surprising, and might try it too. 🙂

grounding: After an appraisal and a rent increase, an employee reopens the budget, raises savings by half of the raise and trims subscriptions.

subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about irregular expenses [Pitfall]
passage: Kunal from the accounts desk here. I sit near Rekha, and I'll describe what I saw this winter without claiming to know what went on inside. In January Rekha proudly showed me a monthly budget that looked perfect: rent, groceries, transport, savings. Then an insurance premium arrived, then festival gifts for relatives, then a laptop repair in the same quarter. None of them were in the sheet. Rekha went quiet at lunch and skipped the canteen for a few days. I saw the sheet again in March and the savings column had been used to cover the gap. Rekha said only, "These costs come every year, I just forgot them." I can't say how it felt, but it did not look easy.

qa.q: Which three expenses arrived in the same quarter and were not in the sheet?
qa.a: An insurance premium, festival gifts for relatives and a laptop repair arrived and were not in the sheet.

qa.q: What might Rekha have been feeling when saying the costs come every year?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt embarrassed or upset, since Rekha went quiet and said the costs were simply forgotten, though Kunal cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Rekha add to the budget, and why?
qa.a: Rekha could list the yearly costs and set aside a small amount each month for them, because lumpy costs then stop breaking the plan.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Rekha's situation from the next desk?
qa.a: Kunal saw Rekha's quiet days and the used savings and feels concerned, but admits not knowing what Rekha felt inside.

grounding: A budget that covers monthly costs but leaves out annual items breaks when several such bills fall in one quarter.
